NEW YORK (CNN) — The *New York Times* endorsed Arizona Sen. John McCain for the Republican presidential nomination over Rudy Giuliani and the rest of the GOP field, while sharply criticizing the former mayor of its home city.

Sens. John McCain, left, and Rudy Giuliani participated in a debate in Florida on Thursday.

In endorsements posted on its Web site for Friday’s editions, the *Times* also backed New York Sen. Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination.

“Senator John McCain of Arizona is the only Republican who promises to end the George Bush style of governing from and on behalf of a small, angry fringe,” the paper’s editorial board wrote. “With a record of working across the aisle to develop sound bipartisan legislation, he would offer a choice to a broader range of Americans than the rest of the Republican field.”

The endorsement anticipated questions from readers about how the New York paper could reject Giuliani, whom it had endorsed for re-election in 1997 and praised for his efforts to reduce crime in the city, as well as for his leadership during the September 11, 2001, attacks.

“That man is not running for president,” the paper wrote. “The Rudolph Giuliani of 2008 first shamelessly turned the horror of 9/11 into a lucrative business, with a secret client list, then exploited his city’s and the country’s nightmare to promote his presidential campaign,” the paper wrote, describing Giuliani as “a narrow, obsessively secretive, vindictive man.”

Giuliani downplayed the harsh criticism, suggesting that the *Times* has a liberal editorial staff that had often disapproved of him.

“I probably never did anything the *New York Times* suggested I do in eight years as mayor of New York City, and if I did, I wouldn’t be considered a conservative Republican,” Giuliani said during a Republican debate Thursday night hosted by MSNBC in Boca Raton, Florida. “I changed welfare, I changed quality of life, I took on homelessness — I did all the things that they think makes you mean and I believe show true compassion and true love for people.”

His was not the only Republican campaign to adopt that approach. An e-mail from the campaign of former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney sarcastically noted that McCain had been endorsed by “[t]hat bastion of conservative advocacy.”

Despite calling McCain a “genuine war hero” and a “staunch advocate of campaign finance reform,” the editorial was far from unreserved praise.

“Mr. McCain was one of the first prominent Republicans to point out how badly the war in Iraq was being managed. We wish he could now see as clearly past the temporary victories produced by Mr. Bush’s unsustainable escalation, which have not led to any change in Iraq’s murderous political calculus,” it read. “At the least, he owes Americans a real idea of how he would win this war, which he says he can do.”

The paper praised Clinton’s chief rival, Sen. Barack Obama, but described Clinton as more qualified for the office.

“It is unfair, especially after seven years of Mr. Bush’s inept leadership, but any Democrat will face tougher questioning about his or her fitness to be commander in chief,” it read. “Mrs. Clinton has more than cleared that bar, using her years in the Senate well to immerse herself in national security issues, and has won the respect of world leaders and many in the American military.”

The Democratic editorial contrasted Clinton and Obama, calling her “the brilliant if at times harsh-sounding senator from New York” and him “the incandescent if still undefined senator from Illinois.”

The paper said Clinton “sometimes overstates the importance of [her] resume,” but added that, upon hearing “her policies and answers for America’s big problems, we are hugely impressed by the depth of her knowledge, by the force of her intellect and by the breadth of, yes, her experience.”

New York is among the many states set to vote in the February 5 Super Tuesday primaries.

NEW YORK (CNN) — The New York Times backed Arizona Senator John McCain for the Republican presidential nomination, choosing him over Rudy Giuliani and the other GOP candidates while delivering sharp criticism of the former mayor of New York City.

McCain and Giuliani appeared Thursday in a debate in Florida. In endorsements published on the newspaper’s website for its Friday editions, the Times also supported New York Senator Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination.

The Times editorial board wrote that McCain was “the only Republican” offering to move away from what it described as George W. Bush’s governing approach, which it said served “a small, angry fringe.” The board said McCain’s history of cooperating with Democrats to craft bipartisan legislation would make him appealing to a wider group of voters than the rest of the Republican field.

The editorial acknowledged that readers might wonder why the New York-based paper was rejecting Giuliani, whom it had endorsed for re-election in 1997 and had previously commended for reducing crime in the city and for his leadership during the September 11, 2001, attacks.

“That man is not running for president,” the Times wrote. It said the 2008 version of Giuliani had “shamelessly” turned the tragedy of 9/11 into a profitable enterprise with undisclosed clients, then used the suffering of New York and the nation to advance his White House campaign. The paper described him as “a narrow, obsessively secretive, vindictive man.”

Giuliani brushed aside the attack, arguing that the Times’ editorial board was liberal and had frequently opposed him. Speaking Thursday night during an MSNBC-hosted Republican debate in Boca Raton, Florida, he said he likely never followed the Times’ advice during his eight years as New York mayor, adding that if he had, he would not be viewed as a conservative Republican. Giuliani said he transformed welfare, improved quality of life, confronted homelessness, and pursued policies the Times considered harsh but that he believed reflected genuine compassion and concern for people.

Other Republican campaigns responded similarly. Mitt Romney’s campaign sent an e-mail mockingly referring to the Times as “[t]hat bastion of conservative advocacy” after its endorsement of McCain.

Even while endorsing McCain, the editorial was not entirely complimentary. It called him a “genuine war hero” and a firm supporter of campaign finance reform, but criticized his position on Iraq. The paper noted that McCain had been among the first major Republicans to recognize how poorly the Iraq War was being handled. However, it said it wished he could look beyond the temporary gains from President Bush’s troop increase, which the Times described as unsustainable and as having failed to alter Iraq’s deadly political dynamics. At minimum, the editorial said, McCain owed voters a concrete explanation of how he would win the war, as he claimed he could.

On the Democratic side, the Times praised Senator Barack Obama, Clinton’s main opponent, but concluded that Clinton was better prepared for the presidency. The editorial said that, unfairly or not, especially after seven years of what it called Bush’s ineffective leadership, any Democratic nominee would face tougher scrutiny over whether he or she was fit to serve as commander in chief. The Times argued that Clinton had more than met that standard, citing her Senate work on national security issues and saying she had gained the respect of foreign leaders and many members of the U.S. military.

The Democratic endorsement compared the two candidates by describing Clinton as “the brilliant if at times harsh-sounding senator from New York” and Obama as “the incandescent if still undefined senator from Illinois.” The paper said Clinton occasionally exaggerated the significance of her résumé, but added that her policy positions and responses to major national problems left the board deeply impressed by her knowledge, intellect and, indeed, experience.

New York is among the many states scheduled to vote in the February 5 Super Tuesday primaries.

**The New York Times endorses McCain, Clinton for 2008 nominations**

*By [Your Name], CNN-style report*

The New York Times endorsed Sen. John McCain for the Republican presidential nomination and Sen. Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination, giving two veteran lawmakers a prominent boost as the 2008 race moved toward key primary contests.

In its Republican endorsement, the Times editorial board praised McCain, the Arizona senator, as the strongest candidate in the GOP field, citing his experience, independence and record on issues such as national security and ethics reform. The paper sharply criticized several of his rivals, arguing that McCain offered the most credible leadership among Republicans seeking the White House.

For the Democratic nomination, the Times backed Clinton, the New York senator and former first lady, calling her highly qualified and emphasizing her command of policy and experience in government. The editorial described Clinton as prepared to lead on domestic and foreign policy issues, while also acknowledging the historic nature and political energy surrounding Sen. Barack Obama’s campaign.

The endorsements came at a pivotal moment in the primary calendar, with Republicans battling in Florida and Democrats looking ahead to a series of major contests.

McCain’s campaign welcomed the endorsement as a sign of his appeal beyond the party’s conservative base, though support from the Times — often viewed skeptically by Republican primary voters — was also quickly used by opponents to question his conservative credentials.

Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor who had staked much of his campaign on Florida, downplayed the endorsement. His campaign suggested that backing from the Times was not likely to sway Republican voters and argued that Giuliani remained the candidate best prepared to handle national security and executive leadership.

Mitt Romney’s campaign also sought to turn the endorsement into a liability for McCain. Romney aides argued that the Times’ support reflected McCain’s positions on issues where he had broken with many conservatives, including campaign finance, immigration and taxes. The Romney campaign portrayed the endorsement as further evidence that McCain was more acceptable to liberal editorial boards than to the Republican base.

On the Democratic side, Clinton’s campaign pointed to the endorsement as validation of her experience and readiness for the presidency. The Times’ support was especially notable because Clinton represented New York in the Senate, giving the endorsement added symbolic weight in her home-state political orbit.

The endorsements did not guarantee victory for either candidate, but they added another high-profile marker in a campaign defined by volatile momentum, shifting alliances and increasingly sharp contrasts between experience, ideology and electability.

**The New York Times Endorses McCain and Clinton, Delivering Sharp Rebuke to Giuliani**

*January 2008 — New York*

The New York Times entered the presidential primary fray this week with endorsements of Senator John McCain of Arizona for the Republican nomination and Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton of New York for the Democratic nomination, using its influential editorial page not only to praise its chosen candidates but to issue a blistering condemnation of former New York City mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani.

The endorsements, published as the presidential race moved toward the pivotal Florida primary and the delegate-rich contests of early February, reflected the newspaper’s view that both parties faced stark choices about leadership, judgment and the nation’s direction after seven years of the Bush administration. While the paper found reservations with both McCain and Clinton, it described them as the strongest and most prepared candidates in their respective fields.

But the most dramatic language was reserved for Giuliani, whose campaign had built much of its national identity on his leadership after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and his two terms as mayor of New York. The Times editorial board, long critical of Giuliani’s mayoralty and his presidential bid, argued that he was unfit for the presidency, portraying his campaign as divisive, authoritarian in temperament and built on an inflated version of his record.

The editorial amounted to a striking hometown rejection of Giuliani, once widely regarded as the national Republican front-runner and still the best-known candidate in the race because of his post-9/11 reputation. Coming from New York’s most prominent newspaper, the rebuke carried symbolic force, even if Giuliani’s support had already weakened after disappointing showings in Iowa, New Hampshire, Michigan and South Carolina.

### A Hometown Paper Turns on Giuliani

The Times’ criticism of Giuliani was sweeping. The editorial board accused the former mayor of running a campaign centered too heavily on fear and national security, while failing to offer a broad or convincing vision for the country. It suggested that his reputation as “America’s mayor” had obscured what the paper saw as a troubling record in office: combative governance, disdain for dissent and poor judgment in key administrative decisions.

The board faulted Giuliani for what it described as a harsh and divisive approach to politics, saying his mayoralty had often been marked by confrontation rather than consensus. It also questioned his use of the September 11 attacks as the central credential for his candidacy, arguing that leadership in a crisis did not erase deeper concerns about temperament, policy and management.

The endorsement editorial revisited issues that had dogged Giuliani for years in New York: his strained relations with minority communities, his battles with civil liberties advocates, and his tendency to centralize power around loyalists. The Times also pointed to questions about his post-mayoral business dealings and his judgment in surrounding himself with controversial associates, including former New York police commissioner Bernard Kerik, whose legal troubles had become a major embarrassment for Giuliani.

In the paper’s view, Giuliani’s candidacy represented the wrong direction for the Republican Party and the country. The Times suggested that after years of war, executive overreach and partisan division, the nation did not need a president whose political style appeared rooted in confrontation and fear.

### Why McCain

Against that backdrop, the Times endorsed McCain as the Republican candidate most capable of moving his party and the nation away from what the editorial board described as the failures of the Bush years.

The endorsement was not without qualification. The paper sharply disagreed with McCain on the Iraq war, noting that he had been among the most persistent defenders of the troop surge and of continuing the American military commitment there. For an editorial page that had long opposed the war, that was no small concern.

Still, the Times argued that McCain stood apart from the rest of the Republican field because of his independence, seriousness and willingness to challenge party orthodoxy. The board cited his record on campaign finance reform, his opposition to torture, his earlier efforts to pursue immigration reform, and his occasional breaks with conservative dogma as evidence that he possessed both political courage and a broader conception of national interest.

The paper also emphasized McCain’s experience in foreign affairs and national security, while contrasting his approach with what it saw as the narrower, more fear-driven appeals of Giuliani. McCain, the board suggested, had a deeper understanding of war and sacrifice, shaped by his years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam and decades in the Senate.

The endorsement framed McCain as a flawed but honorable choice: a Republican with whom the paper often disagreed, but one who had demonstrated independence and a capacity to govern beyond party slogans. In a field that included Giuliani, former Massachusetts governor Mitt Romney, former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee and others, the Times concluded that McCain offered the best hope for a more responsible Republican nomination.

Romney was criticized for shifting positions on major issues, including abortion and social policy, in ways that raised questions about conviction. Huckabee, though praised in some quarters for his populist tone, was viewed as too closely tied to religious conservatism and insufficiently prepared on national policy. Giuliani, however, received the harshest treatment, as the board made clear that it considered his nomination unacceptable.

### Why Clinton

On the Democratic side, the Times endorsed Clinton over Senator Barack Obama of Illinois and former senator John Edwards of North Carolina, calling her the candidate best prepared to govern and the most capable of turning Democratic priorities into law.

The endorsement came at a tense moment in the Democratic contest. Clinton had won New Hampshire after Obama’s breakthrough victory in Iowa, and the race had become a fierce struggle over experience, change and electability. Obama had inspired large crowds with his call for a new politics, while Edwards had continued to emphasize economic inequality and corporate power. Clinton, meanwhile, argued that she possessed the knowledge and toughness to repair the damage of the Bush era from her first day in office.

The Times sided with that argument. Its editorial board praised Clinton’s command of policy, her experience in Washington, and her long engagement with issues such as health care, children’s welfare, women’s rights and national security. The paper said she had demonstrated resilience, discipline and a deep understanding of how government works.

Health care figured prominently in the reasoning. Clinton’s failed attempt to pass universal health coverage during her husband’s administration remained a controversial part of her record, but the Times viewed it as evidence of ambition and commitment rather than disqualification. Her 2008 health care plan, the board suggested, was more comprehensive than Obama’s and reflected a serious attempt to address one of the country’s central domestic problems.

The editorial also credited Clinton with being a strong advocate for the middle class and for restoring competence after the Bush administration. The paper pointed to her Senate work, her policy fluency and her ability to navigate the levers of power as reasons to believe she could be an effective president.

At the same time, the Times acknowledged concerns about Clinton. Her vote authorizing the Iraq war remained a major liability among Democratic voters, and the editorial board did not ignore it. Nor did it dismiss concerns about the polarizing legacy of the Clinton years or the possibility that her candidacy could revive old partisan battles. But the paper concluded that she had learned from experience and was better prepared than her rivals to enact a Democratic agenda.

### Obama Praised, But Passed Over

The endorsement was respectful toward Obama, whose campaign had electrified many Democrats and independents. The Times recognized his intelligence, eloquence and ability to inspire voters disillusioned with Washington. It acknowledged the historic nature of his candidacy and the appeal of his promise to transcend partisan divisions.

Yet the editorial board judged that Obama had not matched Clinton in experience or policy depth. The paper suggested that while his message of change was powerful, Clinton had shown a more detailed grasp of the machinery of government and a clearer ability to deliver results.

That distinction—between inspiration and execution—lay at the heart of the Times’ Democratic endorsement. The board did not reject Obama’s vision, but it argued that Clinton was better equipped for the presidency at that moment.

Edwards, too, received some recognition for focusing attention on poverty, inequality and the influence of corporations. But the paper did not view him as the strongest nominee, particularly compared with Clinton’s breadth of experience and Obama’s political movement.

### The Timing and Impact

The Times’ endorsements arrived at a crucial stage of the campaign. For Republicans, Florida loomed as a decisive test, particularly for Giuliani, who had largely bypassed the early states in hopes of reviving his campaign there. His strategy depended on a strong showing among Florida Republicans, including retirees and transplanted Northeastern voters familiar with his mayoral record.

A harsh rejection from the New York Times was unlikely to sway conservative voters who already distrusted the paper’s editorial page. Indeed, Giuliani’s campaign could attempt to use the endorsement against McCain by portraying the Arizona senator as the favorite of a liberal newspaper. But the intensity of the criticism underscored a larger problem for Giuliani: the gap between his national image and the more complicated assessment of those who had watched him govern up close.

For McCain, the endorsement offered validation from an unexpected quarter. Although Times support was not necessarily an asset in a Republican primary, the editorial reinforced his brand as the independent-minded candidate in the race. It also aligned with his effort to present himself as the most serious and tested Republican contender at a moment when Romney was attacking him from the right and Giuliani was fighting to remain viable.

For Clinton, the endorsement was more plainly useful. As New York’s junior senator, she had a long and sometimes complicated relationship with the state’s dominant newspaper. The Times’ support gave her campaign an establishment seal of approval as she battled Obama for momentum heading into the next contests. It affirmed her central argument: that Democrats should choose experience, toughness and policy mastery over the promise of a less defined political transformation.

### A Broader Editorial Message

Beyond the individual endorsements, the Times’ editorials amounted to a statement about what the newspaper believed the 2008 election should be about. The board called for a break from the Bush administration’s approach to executive power, foreign policy, civil liberties and domestic governance. It favored candidates who, in its view, showed seriousness about repairing institutions, restoring credibility abroad and addressing long-neglected problems at home.

That framework explains the pairing of McCain and Clinton, two senators with long national résumés, reputations for toughness and deep familiarity with Washington. They came from opposing parties and differed sharply on many policies, especially Iraq. But the Times presented each as the most substantial and prepared figure in a crowded field.

It also explains the severity of the paper’s rejection of Giuliani. To the editorial board, Giuliani did not represent renewal, moderation or steadiness. He represented, in its judgment, a politics of fear and division at a time when the country needed the opposite.

Whether voters would heed that judgment was another matter. Newspaper endorsements still carried weight in 2008, particularly among engaged primary voters, but their influence was uneven and often limited by partisan distrust. The Times’ Republican endorsement could even prove double-edged for McCain among conservatives suspicious of media approval.

Still, the endorsements captured a significant moment in the campaign. The Republican contest was unsettled, the Democratic race increasingly intense, and the country was preparing for its first presidential election in decades without an incumbent president or vice president on the ballot.

In endorsing McCain and Clinton, the New York Times chose experience over novelty, policy command over outsider appeal and institutional repair over ideological purity. And in its denunciation of Rudy Giuliani, the paper delivered one of the campaign season’s most pointed editorial judgments: that the man who had built a presidential candidacy on leadership in New York had failed to persuade New York’s most prominent newspaper that he should lead the nation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a detailed news-style account of how the New York Times editorial board evaluated the 2008 presidential candidates, why it rejected Rudy Giuliani, and why it backed McCain and Clinton.
counterfactuals.output:
The New York Times editorial board’s 2008 primary endorsements amounted to a pointed intervention in both parties’ nominating contests: it urged Republicans to choose Senator John McCain of Arizona over the party’s more ideological or polarizing contenders, and Democrats to nominate Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton of New York over a strong field that included Senator Barack Obama and former Senator John Edwards. In doing so, the board also issued a sharp rebuke to former New York mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani, once considered a Republican front-runner and the candidate with the closest geographic and historical connection to the paper.

## How the board framed the 2008 race

The Times treated the 2008 election as an unusually consequential contest taking place after what it saw as the failures of the George W. Bush years: the Iraq war, damage to America’s international standing, expanded executive power, economic strains, health-care insecurity, and a degraded national political climate.

Its editorial-board evaluations emphasized several recurring standards:

- **Judgment and seriousness on national security**
- **Respect for constitutional limits and civil liberties**
- **Capacity to govern competently**
- **Independence from party orthodoxy**
- **Willingness to address climate change, immigration, health care and fiscal policy**
- **Temperament and ability to unite rather than inflame**
- **Depth of policy knowledge and executive credibility**

The board did not claim that either endorsed candidate was ideal. Rather, it argued that McCain and Clinton were the strongest choices within their respective party fields.

## Why the Times rejected Rudy Giuliani

The Times’ rejection of Rudy Giuliani was especially emphatic because Giuliani had entered the race as “America’s mayor,” basing much of his national appeal on his leadership after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. The editorial board acknowledged that Giuliani’s conduct in the immediate aftermath of 9/11 had helped steady New York and the country. But it argued that his presidential campaign had reduced that moment into a political credential invoked too often and examined too little.

The board’s criticism of Giuliani centered on several points.

### 1. It said Giuliani’s campaign relied excessively on 9/11

The Times argued that Giuliani’s national candidacy was built disproportionately on the symbolic capital of Sept. 11. In the board’s view, Giuliani treated the attacks not as one part of a broader record, but as the core justification for his presidency.

The board also suggested that the 9/11 record was more complicated than Giuliani’s campaign allowed. His leadership after the attacks was real, but questions remained about emergency preparedness, communications failures, and decisions made before and after the attacks, including the placement of the city’s emergency command center at 7 World Trade Center.

### 2. It criticized his temperament and governing style

The editorial board had long viewed Giuliani as a combative, polarizing figure. As mayor, he was credited with presiding over falling crime and a revived city, but he was also criticized for authoritarian tendencies, racial tensions, battles with critics, and a disdainful attitude toward dissent.

The Times argued that the country did not need a president with a temperament marked by grievance, confrontation and secrecy—especially after an administration it believed had already expanded executive power too aggressively.

### 3. It found his policy preparation thin

Although Giuliani campaigned as a strong national-security candidate, the board questioned the depth of his knowledge and judgment on foreign policy. It portrayed him as rhetorically hawkish but not sufficiently thoughtful about the complexities of war, terrorism and diplomacy.

On domestic issues, the board saw Giuliani as having moved rightward to satisfy Republican primary voters, especially on taxes, judges, gun rights and social issues. It regarded those shifts as opportunistic and unconvincing.

### 4. It highlighted ethical and managerial concerns

The board also pointed to questions surrounding Giuliani’s business dealings, consulting work, associations, and secrecy about records from his mayoralty. Giuliani Partners had made him wealthy after he left City Hall, but the board saw potential conflicts and insufficient transparency.

His personal life and the public drama surrounding it were not the core objection, but they contributed to the board’s larger concern about judgment, discipline and candor.

### 5. It saw him as the wrong answer to the Bush era

Above all, the Times viewed Giuliani as a candidate who would continue and intensify the politics of fear, executive power and national-security absolutism that it associated with the Bush administration. For the board, Giuliani was not merely unpersuasive; he represented a style of politics it believed the country needed to move beyond.

## Why the Times backed John McCain

The board endorsed John McCain for the Republican nomination while making clear that it disagreed with him on major issues, most notably his support for the Iraq war and many conservative economic positions. Still, among Republican candidates, it judged him the most qualified, independent and responsible.

### 1. McCain had a record of independence

The Times emphasized McCain’s willingness to break with Republican orthodoxy. It cited his work on campaign-finance reform, immigration reform, climate change, opposition to torture, and efforts to curb wasteful spending.

That independence mattered greatly to the board. In a Republican field that included more rigid conservatives and candidates who seemed to be pandering to the party’s base, McCain appeared to the Times as the one contender most willing to put national interest above party discipline.

### 2. He had credibility on national security

Although the board strongly opposed McCain’s continued support for the Iraq war, it respected his seriousness on military and foreign-policy issues. McCain’s personal history as a prisoner of war in Vietnam was not treated merely as biography; it informed the board’s view that he understood war’s costs and had moral standing on issues such as torture and detainee treatment.

The Times was sharply critical of the Bush administration’s interrogation policies, and McCain’s opposition to torture distinguished him from many Republicans.

### 3. He supported immigration reform

McCain’s work with Senator Edward Kennedy on comprehensive immigration reform was a major point in his favor. At a time when Republican primary politics had turned sharply anti-immigration, the board saw McCain’s position as humane, practical and politically courageous.

### 4. He took climate change seriously

McCain’s support for action on global warming also separated him from much of the Republican field. The Times editorial board regarded climate change as a central policy challenge and credited McCain for acknowledging the problem and supporting market-based approaches to reducing emissions.

### 5. The board saw him as the strongest Republican corrective

The endorsement was not an embrace of the Republican Party’s platform, nor a full endorsement of McCain’s worldview. It was a comparative judgment. The Times believed McCain was the Republican most likely to restore some measure of seriousness, restraint and honor to a party the board saw as having been distorted by the Bush presidency.

## Why the Times backed Hillary Clinton

On the Democratic side, the Times endorsed Hillary Clinton, praising the strength of the Democratic field but concluding that Clinton was the best prepared to become president.

The board’s endorsement came at a moment when Barack Obama was energizing voters with a message of generational change and post-partisan politics. The Times acknowledged Obama’s intelligence, eloquence and promise, and it credited John Edwards for focusing the campaign on poverty and economic inequality. But it concluded that Clinton had the strongest combination of experience, policy mastery and ability to govern immediately.

### 1. Clinton had deep policy knowledge

The board stressed Clinton’s command of issues, from health care to foreign policy to economic regulation. It viewed her as a candidate who had learned from both success and failure, including her controversial experience leading the Clinton administration’s 1990s health-care effort.

By 2008, the board saw her as more disciplined, more pragmatic and more knowledgeable than she had been in earlier national fights.

### 2. Health care was central

The Times gave significant weight to Clinton’s commitment to universal health care. Health reform had been one of her defining issues, and the board regarded her plan as more comprehensive than Obama’s because it included an individual mandate to achieve broader coverage.

For a board that had long supported universal coverage, Clinton’s persistence on health care was a major asset.

### 3. It valued her experience in government

Clinton’s years as first lady, senator from New York, and national political figure were central to the endorsement. The board argued that she knew how Washington worked, had been tested by intense opposition, and had shown resilience.

Her Senate tenure also mattered. Representing New York after 9/11, she had worked on homeland security, recovery funding and military issues, and had won respect from some colleagues who had once viewed her skeptically.

### 4. It believed she could repair government after Bush

The Times’ editorial board wanted a president who could quickly reverse Bush-era policies on executive power, civil liberties, foreign relations, science, regulation and domestic investment. It saw Clinton as someone with the competence and toughness to begin that work immediately.

### 5. It judged Obama inspiring but less tested

The board did not dismiss Obama; it described him as a remarkable political talent whose campaign had inspired many voters. But it saw him as less experienced and less specific in some policy areas than Clinton. His promise of unity appealed to many Democrats, but the board was more persuaded by Clinton’s demonstrated familiarity with the machinery of government.

## The broader message of the endorsements

Taken together, the Times’ 2008 primary endorsements reflected a desire to move away from what it regarded as the excesses of the Bush era: unilateralism abroad, fear-based politics, secrecy, weakened civil liberties and ideological rigidity.

- **Giuliani**, in the board’s view, embodied too much of that politics: authoritarian in style, overly reliant on 9/11, thin on policy and inclined toward confrontation.
- **McCain** represented, within the Republican Party, the best available alternative: independent, serious, resistant to torture, willing to address immigration and climate change, though still wrong in the board’s view on Iraq.
- **Clinton** represented, within the Democratic Party, preparation and competence: a candidate with policy depth, resilience and a detailed agenda, especially on health care and restoring effective government.

The endorsements were thus less about ideological symmetry than about comparative judgment. The Times backed the Democrat it believed was most ready to govern and the Republican it believed was most capable of rescuing his party from its worst impulses.
